verses.text: Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God.
Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged of you, or of man’s judgment: yea, I judge not mine own self.
For I know nothing by myself; yet am I not hereby justified: but he that judgeth me is the Lord.

Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come, who both will bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts: and then shall every man have praise of God.

And these things, brethren, I have in a figure transferred to myself and to Apollos for your sakes; that ye might learn in us not to think of men above that which is written, that no one of you be puffed up for one against another.
For who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?
Now ye are full, now ye are rich, ye have reigned as kings without us: and I would to God ye did reign, that we also might reign with you.
For I think that God hath set forth us the apostles last, as it were appointed to death: for we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men.
We are fools for Christ’s sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong; ye are honourable, but we are despised.
Even unto this present hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace;
And labour, working with our own hands: being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it:
Being defamed, we intreat: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day.
I write not these things to shame you, but as my beloved sons I warn you.
For though ye have ten thousand instructers in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel.
Wherefore I beseech you, be ye followers of me.

For this cause have I sent unto you Timotheus, who is my beloved son, and faithful in the Lord, who shall bring you into remembrance of my ways which be in Christ, as I teach every where in every church.
Now some are puffed up, as though I would not come to you.
But I will come to you shortly, if the Lord will, and will know, not the speech of them which are puffed up, but the power.
For the kingdom of God is not in word, but in power.
What will ye? shall I come unto you with a rod, or in love, and in the spirit of meekness?

summary: Paul closes his argument against the Corinthian party spirit by fixing the apostles in their proper place: "Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God." A steward owns nothing and answers to his master, so only one demand is made of him — "Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful." That single standard dissolves the habit of ranking teachers, and Paul refuses the Corinthians' verdict and even his own: "with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged of you, or of man’s judgment: yea, I judge not mine own self." A clean conscience settles nothing, since "I know nothing by myself; yet am I not hereby justified: but he that judgeth me is the Lord." The real verdict waits — "judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come, who both will bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts: and then shall every man have praise of God." Paul then names his method, that "these things, brethren, I have in a figure transferred to myself and to Apollos for your sakes; that ye might learn in us not to think of men above that which is written, that no one of you be puffed up for one against another," and drives at the root of the factions with three questions: "who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?" Everything they boast in arrived as a gift, so the boasting is incoherent. Irony follows — "Now ye are full, now ye are rich, ye have reigned as kings without us: and I would to God ye did reign, that we also might reign with you" — and against that imagined enthronement Paul sets the apostles' actual position, "last, as it were appointed to death: for we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men." The contrast is laid out in pairs: "We are fools for Christ’s sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong; ye are honourable, but we are despised." The catalogue that follows is physical and unglamorous — they "hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace," they "labour, working with our own hands," and their response to hostility reverses it: "being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it: Being defamed, we intreat," until they are "made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day." Then the tone turns paternal. "I write not these things to shame you, but as my beloved sons I warn you. For though ye have ten thousand instructers in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel." On that ground alone he can say "be ye followers of me," and he sends Timotheus, "my beloved son, and faithful in the Lord," to "bring you into remembrance of my ways which be in Christ, as I teach every where in every church." To those "puffed up, as though I would not come to you," he promises a visit that will test substance rather than rhetoric: "I will come to you shortly, if the Lord will, and will know, not the speech of them which are puffed up, but the power. For the kingdom of God is not in word, but in power." The chapter ends by handing them the choice: "What will ye? shall I come unto you with a rod, or in love, and in the spirit of meekness?"
takeaways: Ministry is defined here by stewardship rather than by ownership or celebrity. Paul asks only that he be accounted one of "the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God," and a steward is by definition handling what belongs to someone else. That is why the measure applied to him is not eloquence, results, or popularity but a single quality — "it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful." The Corinthians were grading their teachers like patrons grading orators; Paul answers that the goods were never his to be praised for, and that the only relevant question about a steward is whether he was true to the master's intent with the master's property.

The chapter installs a deliberate reserve about verdicts, including verdicts on oneself. Paul treats the church's opinion of him as "a very small thing," and then goes further: "yea, I judge not mine own self. For I know nothing by myself; yet am I not hereby justified." A quiet conscience is evidence, not acquittal, because self-knowledge is partial and the court is not one's own. The instruction that follows — "judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come" — is not a ban on discernment, since Paul issues sharp judgments a chapter later, but a ban on premature final verdicts about persons whose hidden motives only God can read. Notably, the outcome he expects from that disclosure is generous: "then shall every man have praise of God."

The three questions of verse seven cut the nerve of every rivalry in the letter: "who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?" Paul does not deny that the Corinthians have real gifts, real teachers, and real knowledge. He denies that any of it originated with them. Boasting in a gift is a category error, treating a received thing as an achievement, and once that is seen, being "puffed up for one against another" collapses on its own without needing any further argument.

Paul's irony exposes a church that thinks it has already arrived. "Now ye are full, now ye are rich, ye have reigned as kings without us" describes a community living as though the age of glory had come early, and his wistful reply — "I would to God ye did reign, that we also might reign with you" — concedes the hope while denying the timing. The apostolic reality is the opposite shape: "last, as it were appointed to death," a "spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men," hungry, homeless, "the offscouring of all things." The pattern of authentic ministry is cruciform, and the sign of it is the reversal in their conduct — "being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it: Being defamed, we intreat."

Against a market of teachers Paul asserts a relationship that cannot be duplicated: "though ye have ten thousand instructers in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel." Instruction can be shopped for, but the one through whom the gospel first gave them life stands in a different relation entirely, which is why he can follow it with "be ye followers of me" without arrogance. The fatherhood is exercised as warning rather than shaming — "I write not these things to shame you, but as my beloved sons I warn you" — and it is handed on through a person, Timotheus, who will "bring you into remembrance of my ways which be in Christ, as I teach every where in every church." The content taught at Corinth is not a local variant but the same teaching given everywhere.

The closing test is between talk and reality: "I will come to you shortly, if the Lord will, and will know, not the speech of them which are puffed up, but the power. For the kingdom of God is not in word, but in power." In a city that prized rhetorical display, Paul says the kingdom will be audited by what it actually effects, not by how impressively it is described. The final question leaves the outcome with the Corinthians rather than with him — "shall I come unto you with a rod, or in love, and in the spirit of meekness?" — so that even apostolic discipline is presented as something their own response determines.

crossRefs.label: Luke 12:42-48 — Who then is that faithful and wise steward... to give them their portion of meat in due season?
crossRefs.why: The parable supplies the picture Paul is working from when he calls the apostles "stewards of the mysteries of God" and insists "it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful." A steward is judged at the master's return, not by the household's opinion in the meantime, which is exactly why Paul can say "judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come."

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 3:6-7,21 — I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase... let no man glory in men
crossRefs.why: Chapter four is the conclusion of an argument begun here, where the same pair of names is used to make the same point. The planting and watering image already reduces the teachers to instruments, and "let no man glory in men" is what verse seven then presses to its root with "what hast thou that thou didst not receive?"

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 11:23-27 — in stripes above measure, in prisons more frequent... in hunger and thirst
crossRefs.why: The later catalogue of hardships expands the one given here in compressed form: "we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace." In both places Paul answers rivals who trade on impressive appearance by listing what looks like disqualification, treating weakness as the credential of a true apostle.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 7:1-2 — Judge not, that ye be not judged
crossRefs.why: Paul's "judge nothing before the time" is often read alongside this saying, and the pairing clarifies both. Neither text forbids discernment, since Paul commands a hard judgment in the very next chapter of this letter; what both forbid is the presumption of rendering a final verdict on a person, which belongs to the one "who both will bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts."

crossRefs.label: Galatians 4:19 — My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you
crossRefs.why: The same paternal language appears there under a maternal image, showing that Paul's claim "in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel" is a settled way of describing his relation to churches he founded, not a one-time rhetorical flourish. Both passages combine deep affection with the willingness to rebuke that affection makes possible.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 23:8-9 — call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven
crossRefs.why: This saying is the standing counterweight to Paul's "ye have not many fathers," and the two texts are the poles of a long dispute over spiritual paternity and titles. Read together they frame the question of whether Paul is claiming something the Lord forbade or exercising a derived fatherhood that points past itself, since his own point is that he begot them only "through the gospel."

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading hears in "stewards of the mysteries of God" a description of the ordained ministry as an entrusted office, and takes the "mysteries" to include the sacraments as well as the revealed saving plan. On this reading Paul is not describing every believer's stewardship of the gospel in general but the particular dispensation committed to those set apart as "the ministers of Christ," who administer holy things that are not their own property and who will answer to the Lord and not to the congregation for how they have handled them. The requirement "that a man be found faithful" is then read as attaching to an office with real authority — the same authority that allows Paul to speak of coming "with a rod" — while the office itself remains wholly instrumental, since the mysteries belong to God.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally take "the mysteries of God" here in continuity with Paul's earlier use in this letter, where the mystery is the hidden wisdom of God now revealed in the crucified Christ, so that stewardship means above all the faithful preaching and safeguarding of that gospel. On this reading the accent falls on the word entrusted rather than on sacramental administration, ministers are servants of that word rather than holders of a sacerdotal office, and the whole passage cuts against clerical status precisely by describing ministers as dispensable stewards of goods belonging to another. Both traditions agree that the minister owns nothing he dispenses, that his accountability runs to the Lord rather than to the congregation's estimate, and that fidelity rather than impressiveness is the only measure that will finally count.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic tradition reads "in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel" as establishing a genuine spiritual fatherhood, exercised in the Church and derived entirely from God's own fatherhood. Paul distinguishes the many "instructers" from the few "fathers," which implies that teaching alone does not create the bond he has with the Corinthians; something generative happened through his ministry of the gospel that gives him both the right to say "be ye followers of me" and the standing to warn them "as my beloved sons." This is the scriptural warrant traditionally invoked for calling those in pastoral office fathers, on the understanding that the title always names a participation in the Father's paternity rather than a rival to it.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readers point to the Lord's own instruction to "call no man your father upon the earth," and argue that Paul is using an affectionate metaphor for a unique historical relation — he personally founded this church — rather than authorizing an ecclesiastical title. They note that Paul immediately qualifies the claim by grounding it in the gospel itself, that he elsewhere insists neither he nor Apollos is anything, and that the chapter's whole thrust is against elevating human figures, which makes it an odd basis for a permanent honorific. Both traditions affirm that whatever fatherhood Paul claims is derivative and instrumental, that imitation of a minister is legitimate only so far as he imitates Christ, and that the relationship is meant to produce maturity rather than dependence.

interpretationNotes.claim: On the Catholic reading, "not to think of men above that which is written" is a warning against the Corinthians' inflated estimate of their favorite teachers, measured by the scriptural texts Paul has already been citing against human boasting, rather than a formal principle that written Scripture alone is the rule of faith. The immediate object of the phrase is men, not doctrine: the Corinthians are to stop rating Paul and Apollos beyond what the written word allows anyone to claim for a mere servant. The same chapter is read as showing how apostolic teaching was actually transmitted, since Paul sends Timotheus to "bring you into remembrance of my ways which be in Christ, as I teach every where in every church" — a living, personally carried, and uniform apostolic practice held across all the churches.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters read the phrase as placing a written standard over every human estimate, and take it as an early expression of the instinct that Scripture norms the Church's judgments rather than the reverse. They observe that Paul appeals to what is written as the fixed measure at precisely the moment he is dismantling loyalty to personalities, and that his own oral teaching is not set against Scripture but is the apostolic message that would itself be inscribed, so that the "ways which be in Christ" delivered uniformly to every church are the same content now available in the apostolic writings. Both traditions agree that Paul subordinates all human teachers to a standard outside themselves, and that the practical aim of the verse is that "no one of you be puffed up for one against another."

authoring.attributionNotes: Original synthesis grounded in the KJV text and the general Catholic/Christian interpretive tradition. No specific published source is quoted or cited; tradition labels denote a position, not a copied source.
